They are not comparable across models. A different embedding model scoring the same pair at 0.9 has not found more meaning; it has a different scale. Chapter 10 meets this directly, with a measured case where one retrieval system got every question right with a smaller confidence gap than a system that got half of them wrong.

What they are: the sum of 384 products, on two lists that each have length 1, which is a measurement of how nearly two arrows point the same way. That is all, and it is enough to build a search engine on.

Try it 8.4: how much arithmetic is in one of those numbers

The number 0.833303 came out of a dot product between two vectors with D=384D = 384D=384.

(a) How many multiplications were performed? (b) How many additions were performed? (c) The lab compared all six sentences against all six, filling a 6 by 6 grid. How many dot products is that in total, counting every cell of the grid including the diagonal? (d) Roughly how many multiplications is that altogether?

Solution

(a) One multiplication per position, and there are 384 positions. 384 multiplications.

(b) You add 384 products together. Adding 384 numbers takes 383 additions, because the first number does not need to be added to anything; it starts the total. 383 additions.

(c) A 6 by 6 grid has 6×6=366 \times 6 = 366×6=36 cells. 36 dot products. Six of them are a sentence against itself, which is why the grid’s diagonal is all 1s, and the grid is a mirror image of itself across that diagonal, so only 15 of the 36 are genuinely different comparisons.

(d) 36×384=13,82436 \times 384 = 13{,}82436×384=13,824 multiplications.

That is a large number to do by hand and nothing at all for a computer. This is the honest reason the code exists: not because the mathematics is too hard for you, but because there is too much of it. You have done the identical arithmetic twice already in this chapter, with D=2D = 2D=2.

Try it 8.5: predicting a sign before you look

Without running anything, predict the sign, positive or negative, of the dot product between these two sentences from the list above:

“Kern County’s largest city is Bakersfield.”

“The stock market fell sharply on Tuesday.”

Then say whether you expect it to be closer to 0.833303 or to 0.084388, and why. The measured answer is in lab/out/we5_embeddings.json, in row 3 and column 4 of the similarity matrix.

Solution

Prediction. Positive, and small. The two sentences have nothing to do with each other, so there is no reason to expect the arrows to lean together. But both are plain English sentences of similar shape, which was worth 0.084388 for the cat and Kern County pair, so a small positive number is the sensible guess. It should be much nearer 0.084388 than 0.833303.

The measured value is 0.081422. That is recorded in lab/out/we5_embeddings.json, in the similarity matrix at row 3, column 4.

Almost exactly the same as the 0.084388 of the cat and Kern County pair, and the reason is the same: two unrelated English sentences share the general quality of being unrelated English sentences, and the model prices that at about eight hundredths.

If you predicted negative, you were not being unreasonable. Only one pair among the fifteen distinct comparisons came out negative, and reading the sign of a number this close to zero is not a skill worth developing. The distinction that matters is between about 0.08 and about 0.83.

Common mistakes¶

Seven things that go wrong in this chapter, with how to spot each one.

  1. Adding the coordinates instead of squaring them. For (3,4)(3,4)(3,4) this gives 3+4=73 + 4 = 73+4=7 rather than 5. How to spot it: your length is bigger than it should be, and it equals the sum of the coordinates. The straight line between two points is always shorter than a route with a corner in it, so a length of 7 for a journey of 3 then 4 cannot be right.

  2. Forgetting the square root. For (3,4)(3,4)(3,4) this gives 25 rather than 5. How to spot it: your length is much larger than the biggest coordinate. A length is normally in the same neighbourhood as the coordinates, not five times bigger.

  3. Squaring a negative number and keeping the minus sign. Writing (−4)2=−16(-4)^2 = -16(−4)2=−16 instead of 16. How to spot it: your sum of squares comes out negative, or smaller than it should, and then the square root fails or the length is too small. A square is never negative.

  4. Pairing the wrong coordinates in a dot product. Multiplying a1a_1a1​ by b2b_2b2​. For a=(3,4)\mathbf{a} = (3,4)a=(3,4) and b=(4,3)\mathbf{b} = (4,3)b=(4,3) this gives 25 instead of 24, which is close enough to look plausible. How to spot it: check your answer against b⋅a\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{a}b⋅a, computed from scratch. Swapping the vectors cannot change a correct dot product, and it does change a mispaired one.

  5. The Python index shift. Writing vector_a[1] when you mean a1a_1a1​. How to spot it: your code runs happily and gives the wrong answer, which is the worst kind of bug. a1a_1a1​ is vector_a[0], a2a_2a2​ is vector_a[1]. Write it down somewhere you can see it.

  6. Confusing len() with length. len(vector_a) is 2, the count of numbers. ∥a∥\lVert \mathbf{a} \rVert∥a∥ is 5, the reach of the arrow. How to spot it: your “length” comes out as a small whole number that is the same for every 2-D vector you try. If every vector you test has length 2, you have computed len.

  7. Treating a big dot product as proof of strong agreement. a⋅d=50\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 50a⋅d=50 is bigger than a⋅b=24\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 24a⋅b=24, and the reason is that d\mathbf{d}d is twice as long, not that it agrees twice as well. How to spot it: compute the lengths. If one vector is much longer than the other, the raw dot product is not yet a fair comparison. Chapter 9 is the fix.

What to remember¶

A vector is an ordered list of numbers and an arrow from the origin, and those are two ways of holding the same object. The length of the arrow is Pythagoras: square every number, add the squares, take the square root, so (3,4)(3,4)(3,4) has length 9+16=25=5\sqrt{9+16} = \sqrt{25} = 59+16​=25​=5. The dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds the results, giving one number that is positive when two arrows lean the same way, zero when they meet at a right angle, and negative when they lean apart. Every one of these formulas is written with DDD left open, so a list of 384 numbers is handled by the identical arithmetic as a list of 2, which is how a real model scored two sentences sharing no words at 0.612421. The raw dot product still grows when either arrow grows, and removing that size effect is the whole business of Chapter 9.

Practice problems¶

Twenty-six problems in three tiers. Warm-up asks whether you can do the arithmetic. Practice asks whether you can apply it. Stretch asks whether you can reason with it.

Answers to the odd-numbered problems are in the Answers appendix. Every vector invented in these problems is made up for practice unless the problem names a file in lab/out/, in which case the number is a real measurement and you can open the file and check it.

Warm-up¶

  1. Write down the coordinates of the point that is 7 to the right of the origin and 2 below it.

  2. Say which of (5,−2)(5, -2)(5,−2) and (−2,5)(-2, 5)(−2,5) is farther to the right, and which is higher up.

  3. Compute ∥u∥\lVert \mathbf{u} \rVert∥u∥ for u=(6,8)\mathbf{u} = (6, 8)u=(6,8). Show the squaring, the addition and the square root as three separate lines.

  4. Compute ∥u∥\lVert \mathbf{u} \rVert∥u∥ for u=(0,7)\mathbf{u} = (0, 7)u=(0,7).

  5. Compute ∥u∥\lVert \mathbf{u} \rVert∥u∥ for u=(−3,−4)\mathbf{u} = (-3, -4)u=(−3,−4). State what the two minus signs do to the answer.

  6. Compute p⋅q\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{q}p⋅q for p=(2,5)\mathbf{p} = (2, 5)p=(2,5) and q=(3,1)\mathbf{q} = (3, 1)q=(3,1).

  7. Compute p⋅q\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{q}p⋅q for p=(1,0)\mathbf{p} = (1, 0)p=(1,0) and q=(0,1)\mathbf{q} = (0, 1)q=(0,1). Say in one sentence what your answer means about the two arrows.

  8. Compute p⋅q\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{q}p⋅q for p=(4,−2)\mathbf{p} = (4, -2)p=(4,−2) and q=(−1,3)\mathbf{q} = (-1, 3)q=(−1,3).

  9. Compute v⋅v\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}v⋅v for v=(2,3)\mathbf{v} = (2, 3)v=(2,3), then compute ∥v∥\lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert∥v∥ and square it. Confirm that Formula 8.6 holds.

  10. Compute the dot product of the four-dimensional vectors s=(1,2,0,4)\mathbf{s} = (1, 2, 0, 4)s=(1,2,0,4) and t=(3,1,7,2)\mathbf{t} = (3, 1, 7, 2)t=(3,1,7,2). Show all four products and the running total.

Practice¶

  1. Normalise u=(0,5)\mathbf{u} = (0, 5)u=(0,5) using Formula 8.7. Then verify that the length of your answer is exactly 1.

  2. Normalise u=(3,4)\mathbf{u} = (3, 4)u=(3,4) and then normalise d=(6,8)\mathbf{d} = (6, 8)d=(6,8). Compare the two answers and explain in one sentence why they came out the way they did.

  3. Find a vector perpendicular to (7,−2)(7, -2)(7,−2). Prove it is perpendicular with a dot product. Then find a second, different perpendicular vector.

  4. Show that a⋅d=50\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 50a⋅d=50 for a=(3,4)\mathbf{a} = (3,4)a=(3,4) and d=(6,8)\mathbf{d} = (6,8)d=(6,8), that a⋅b=24\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 24a⋅b=24 for b=(4,3)\mathbf{b} = (4,3)b=(4,3), and that a⋅a=25\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 25a⋅a=25. Then explain, in two sentences, why the gap between 50 and 24 is not by itself a measurement of direction. Use the third answer in your explanation: a\mathbf{a}a points in exactly its own direction and still scores only 25, so most of the 50 is length rather than direction.

  5. A vector g\mathbf{g}g has ∥g∥=5\lVert \mathbf{g} \rVert = 5∥g∥=5. Every number in g\mathbf{g}g is then multiplied by 3, giving a new vector h\mathbf{h}h. Without knowing what g\mathbf{g}g's numbers are, state ∥h∥\lVert \mathbf{h} \rVert∥h∥ and explain how you know.

  6. Two vectors have D=384D = 384D=384 and both have length 1. State the largest value their dot product could possibly take, the smallest, and what each of those two extremes would mean about the two sentences.

  7. Open lab/out/we5_embeddings.json and find the similarity matrix. Read off the value in row 0, column 3, and the value in row 3, column 0. Explain why those two numbers are the same.

  8. Using the same file, list the six sentences in order of how similar they are to “Bakersfield is in Kern County, California.”, most similar first. Exclude the sentence’s comparison with itself.

  9. State how many multiplications and how many additions are needed for one dot product between two vectors with D=384D = 384D=384. Then state the same two counts for D=2D = 2D=2, and say what stayed the same between the two cases.

  10. Open the simulation and drag b\mathbf{b}b until the Dot product readout is as close to 0.00 as you can get it. Record the coordinates of b\mathbf{b}b and the Angle readout. Then check your coordinates by computing the dot product by hand.

Stretch¶

  1. Invent two two-dimensional vectors whose dot product is negative, with neither vector having a zero in it. Draw them roughly. Then write one sentence explaining what a negative dot product would be saying if these were two sentences rather than two arrows.

  2. The lab measured the dot product of the stock market sentence and the photosynthesis sentence at -0.016586 (lab/out/we5_embeddings.json, row 4, column 5). Write a short paragraph on what that number does and does not license you to claim. Address in particular whether it means the model believes the two sentences contradict each other.

  3. A classmate says: “384 dimensions means the model has worked out 384 different facts about each sentence.” Write a reply of three or four sentences. Say what is wrong with the claim and what would be a more accurate way to describe the 384 numbers.

  4. Suppose an embedding model did not normalise its output, so that longer sentences came back as longer vectors. Explain, using the a\mathbf{a}a and d\mathbf{d}d example from this chapter, what would go wrong if you ranked search results by raw dot product. Then state what you would need to divide by to repair it. This is the argument Chapter 9 makes in full.

  5. The embedding model in this chapter holds 22,713,216 parameters (lab/out/appendix_python_reference_checks.json, key embed). The retrieval work in Chapter 10 also used bge-small-en-v1.5, which holds 33,360,000 (_research/00-lab-verified-findings.md, section 11). Compute the ratio of the larger to the smaller, to two decimal places. Then, in two sentences, say why a course whose subject is access and resource cost cares about a ratio like that.

  6. Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct holds 494,032,768 parameters (lab/out/we3_params_quant.json) and takes 953 megabytes of disk, while the embedding model in this chapter holds 22,713,216 parameters and takes 87 megabytes (both disk figures from lab/out/appendix_python_reference_checks.json, key disk_usage). Compute both ratios, parameters and megabytes, to one decimal place. The two ratios are not equal. Suggest one reason why the disk figures might not scale exactly with the parameter counts. Chapter 6 has the answer if you want to check yourself.

What is next¶

You now have a number that says how much two arrows agree, and one defect in it: the number grows when an arrow grows, whether or not the direction improved. That defect is fatal for comparing sentences, because a longer sentence is not a better answer.

Chapter 9 repairs it in one step, by dividing by both lengths. The repair has a name, cosine similarity, and the measured case that proves it is needed is already in this chapter: a=(3,4)\mathbf{a} = (3,4)a=(3,4) and d=(6,8)\mathbf{d} = (6,8)d=(6,8) point in precisely the same direction, and their raw dot product is 50 while a\mathbf{a}a with itself is only 25. After the division, both come out at exactly 1.0000.
